Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I think the authors have made a good effort to address the reviewer's concerns and the paper is nearly ready for publication. Nevertheless, I still have a few concerns that I hope the authors can take into account.

Reviewer point 3:

In the abstract, the authors say they "build on" their previous study, but I would argue that they are not building on it, they are correcting a major conclusion from it. Also, in the abstract they say that they "illuminate how γ-TuRC is controlled in space and time in order to build specific cytoskeletal structures" (and this statement is essentially repeated in the first line of the Discussion), but the authors have not studied these aspects at all. This, therefore, needs to be removed/toned down.

Author Response:

These are excellent points raised by the reviewer. We agree that in essence we are correcting a conclusion from our previous study concerning the role of γTuNA on γTuRC activity and consequently, we edited the abstract. As to the spatial-temporal regulation of the level of γTuRC activity, we also agree that most of our data concerning the interaction of γTuNA with γTuRC, the effect on γTuRC activity, and the antagonistic role of stathmin are largely addressing the spatial regulation of microtubule nucleation (MTOC vs cytoplasm). However, previous work has shown that the number of CDK5RAP2 molecules at the centrosome (the most potent MTOC) increases during the transition from interphase to mitosis which results in increased MT nucleation activity via increased γTuRC recruitment (see Piehl et al., PNAS, 2004; Lawo et al., Nat Cell Biol, 2012; and Menella et al., Nat Cell Biol, 2012). Thus, the temporal control of the number of γTuRC binding sites (in interphase vs mitosis) is a method of temporally regulating the level of microtubule nucleation, while simultaneously spatially restricting it. We see our findings here as supportive of the hypothesis that controlling the cellular location and number of γTuNAs over time is a means of spatially and temporally regulating γTuRC microtubule nucleation. On top of that, and critically, we directly show that we can immediately activate γTuRC activity via the addition of dimerized γTuNA, thus showing that the interaction of γTuRC and γTuNA at the centrosome are essentially an intertwined form of spatial and temporal control. To address these points, we edited the discussion in a section on spatio-temporal control (page 18).

New Reviewer Response:

I appreciate the authors additional section in the discussion about the work that others have carried out on the spatiotemporal control of γ-TuRC activation. However, it seems the authors have misunderstood my original point about not showing data on the spatiotemporal regulation of γ-TuRC activation – I did not mean that they had only addressed spatial control; I meant that they had not addressed either spatial or temporal control. This is because their data shows, very nicely, that γ-TuNA binding to γ-TuRCs activates γ-TuRCs but it does not show how γ-TuNA binding to γ-TuRCs is regulated in space and time. The authors appear to propose that spatial control is achieved by localising CDK5RAP2 to centrosomes, but CDK5RAP2 is also present in the cytoplasm and so, in theory, has the potential to bind (and activate) γ-TuRCs in the cytoplasm. As the authors discuss, this binding is likely auto-inhibited by other cis-regulatory elements, but this idea comes from other studies, not this one. And they certainly have not linked this to building "specific cytoskeletal structures". I think the authors should focus their summary statement on what they have actually shown – something more like "In sum, our improved assays finally prove that γ-TuNA binding strongly activates γ-TuRCs, explaining previously observed effects of γ-TuNA expression in cells".

Reviewer point 6:

The authors discuss the idea that the effect of γ-TuNA could be further enhanced by γ-TuRCs being recruited to sites of high local tubulin concentration. Again, this would be easy for them to test, by varying tubulin concentration in their assays and measuring the fold change in γ-TuRCmediated nucleation in mock vs γ-TuNA addition.

Author Response:

We thank the reviewer for their comment. We agree that varying the tubulin concentration is a worthwhile experiment, especially in light of our hypothesis that γTuNA enables γTuRC to nucleate MTs at lower tubulin concentrations than otherwise possible (as suggested by our in vitro experiments using stathmin in Figure 6). While we could increase the tubulin concentration above 15 µM tubulin in the in vitro assay, we do not report higher concentrations in this study as background spontaneous MT nucleation increases such that it can become difficult to distinguish γTuRC-nucleated MTs. Also, at 15 µM tubulin and 1.65 µM γTuNA dimer (3.3 µM monomer γTuNA) we find our assay saturates within 25 seconds, by which time we see a maximum of ~300 MTs per 40 µm by 40 µm area on the coverslip (Figure 5C). This is in agreement with the number of fluorescent γTuRCs we see for the equivalent surface area (mean: 377 MTs; first to third quartile range: 302 to 469 γTuRCs; see Author Response Figure 1). For this reason, we believe that practically all nucleation-competent γTuRCs attached to our coverslips are nucleating MTs within 25 seconds in the presence of 15 μm tubulin and 1.65 µM γTuNA dimer (3.3 µM monomer). Thus 15 µM is the highest we can increase the tubulin concentration in our assays. As a result, we decided to instead decrease our tubulin concentration in the assay, setting it at γTuRC's critical concentration. We then assayed for γTuNA's effect on γTuRC MT nucleation at this low tubulin concentration in vitro (now incorporated into Figure 6, as panel E). In our previous study (Thawani et al., 2020), we found that the critical concentration in the presence of γTuRC was 7 µM tubulin, where γTuRC has very low but still detectable nucleation ability (at least 1 MT nucleated per field during the course of a 5 min experiment). This was also observed by our colleagues in Consolati et al., Dev Cell, 2020 at 7.5 µM tubulin (defined by the authors as at least 1 MT nucleated per 164 µm2 field over 20 min). As shown in Figure 6E, we again validate this finding, observing that our purified γTuRC has very little activity at 7 µM tubulin with only 1 to 2 MTs nucleated per field of view over the course of 5 min (mock buffer condition). These MTs are also short and appear to be more dynamic than those generated by γTuRC at 15 µM tubulin. In Figure 6E, we show all MTs nucleated in our assay at 7 µM tubulin, regardless of lifetime, by presenting max intensity projections for our 5 min time series. Critically, in the presence of 1.65 µM γTuNA dimer (3.3 µM monomer), ~40 γTuRCs nucleate MTs per field despite being at this low tubulin concentration. This is approximately a 25-fold increase in the total number of MTs generated over the entire 5 min assay, as compared to the buffer condition (Figure 6E). Thus, we find further validation that γTuNA enables γTuRC to nucleate MTs even under low, constrained tubulin concentrations, an observation we first described in our experiments with stathmin (Figure 6A-D). We would also like to note that this new experiment is conceptually equivalent to our Figure 6C experiments using 15 µM tubulin and 4 µM stathmin. As 1 molecule of stathmin sequesters 2 tubulin subunits, 4 µM stathmin would leave only ~7 µM tubulin free in a 15 µM tubulin reaction (assuming 100% of the stathmin is functional). The fact that these two experiments agree not only confirms that γTuNA increases γTuRC's efficiency (i.e. lowers γTuRC's critical concentration), but also that stathmin indirectly regulates γTuRC activity by constraining the cytoplasmic tubulin pool.

New Reviewer Response:

I appreciate the extra experiments, but I'm not sure they address the initial point, which was whether "the effect of γ-TuNA could be further enhanced by γ-TuRCs being recruited to sites of high local tubulin concentration", and not whether γ-TuNA promotes microtubule nucleation at low tubulin concentrations (which it clearly does). The authors actually make the point that raising the tubulin concentration in their experiments makes it hard to distinguish the microtubules nucleated by γ-TuRCs from those nucleated spontaneously. From this, I would assume that the effect of γ-TuNA would not be further enhanced when γ-TuRCs are recruited to sites of high local tubulin concentration, because microtubules would simply spontaneously nucleate if the tubulin concentration were high enough. It seems more valid to report that γ-TuNA is required when tubulin concentrations are low.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

As I stated already in my earlier review, I am in favor of this manuscript.

I am a bit disappointed, though, by the manner that this revision has been performed: the authors have provided detailed responses to my concerns in their rebuttal letter (importance of dimerization for gTuRC-binding; gTuNA mutants), but it seems that they haven't significantly addressed these points in the revised manuscript. Similarly, they ignored to discuss related concerns raised by reviewer 3. Our comments were meant to help improving the manuscript! Simply arguing in the rebuttal is not enough…

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior work establishing γTuRC as a 2.2 MDa complex forming an asymmetric ring of γ-tubulin subunits that acts as a template for MT nucleation. The structure is conserved across species despite compositional differences, and the ring's pitch and diameter appear incompatible with the MT lattice, suggesting a conformational change is required for nucleation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are all supported by citations to prior published work and represent established knowledge in the field. These claims provide appropriate background context for the current study and accurately represent the state of knowledge about γTuRC structure and function.

results.result: Prior work has established that Cdk5rap2 recruits γTuRC to the centrosome and Golgi and increases its nucleation activity through the conserved γTuNA (CM1) domain. This domain is conserved across species and found in related proteins including myomegalin and TPX2.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 are supported by multiple citations to prior published work and establish the known role of the γTuNA domain. These claims provide essential background for understanding the significance of the current study's findings.

results.result: Previous studies by the authors and others reported that γTuNA had minimal effect on antibody-purified Xenopus γTuRC activity in vitro, creating an apparent discrepancy with cell-based studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by citations to prior work (Thawani et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020) and accurately describe the motivation for the current study. This establishes the scientific context for why the improved methods described in this manuscript were necessary.

results.result: Wildtype γTuNA triggers up to ~75-fold increase in MT nucleation in Xenopus egg extract, requiring the F75 residue, while having no effect on γTuRC assembly. This validates prior studies showing γTuNA activates MT nucleation in extract.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The titration series, F75A mutant control, and sucrose gradient analysis provide strong evidence for γTuNA's activation effect in extract without affecting γTuRC assembly. Statistical analysis and multiple biological replicates strengthen these findings.

results.result: γTuNA requires γTuRC to activate MT nucleation, as demonstrated by depletion experiments showing >75% loss of γ-tubulin signal and loss of γTuNA's activation effect in depleted extracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1E-F showing Western blot evidence of γTuRC depletion and loss of γTuNA activation effect. The depletion experiment provides direct evidence that γTuRC is the target of γTuNA's activation effect.

results.result: γTuNA-coated beads form large MT asters in extract and in vitro, demonstrating that γTuNA domains are sufficient to specify new sites of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation. The F75A mutant shows severely impaired aster formation, with residual activity attributed to low stringency washes.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2B-C and Video 1, showing MT aster formation from wildtype γTuNA beads but not F75A mutant beads. The explanation for residual F75A activity is supported by Western blot data in supplementary figures showing no γTuRC binding after higher stringency washes.

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that γTuRC is the dominant co-precipitant for wildtype versions of human and Xenopus γTuNA.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, which displays volcano plots and a table of proteins enriched by wildtype γTuNA baits. The data clearly shows γTuRC components as the most abundant co-precipitants.

results.result: Size-exclusion chromatography reveals that wildtype γTuNA is a dimer, with dimerization dependent on residues I67, L70, and L77. The double hydrophilic mutants (I67D/L70D) are entirely monomeric, while F63A and F75A mutations do not affect dimerization. Individual mutations at I67, L70, or L77 produce intermediate populations between dimer and monomer.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are supported by SEC data in Figure 3B-C showing distinct retention volumes for wildtype (dimer) versus mutants. The systematic mutagenesis approach and quantitative analysis of peak retention volumes provide strong evidence for the specific residues required for dimerization.

results.result: Both γTuNA dimerization and the F75 residue are required for binding γTuRC. Monomeric mutants (I67D/L70D, I67D/L70D/L77D) do not bind γTuRC, while intermediate dimer mutants (I67A, L70A, L77A) show correspondingly intermediate levels of γTuRC binding. The F75A mutant does not bind γTuRC despite maintaining dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 are supported by Western blot data in Figure 3D-G showing correlation between dimerization state and γTuRC binding ability. The systematic analysis of multiple mutants with quantification (N=2-3 biological replicates) provides strong evidence that both dimerization and F75 are necessary for γTuRC binding.

results.result: Forcing γTuNA dimerization via addition of a constitutively dimeric GCN4 domain did not rescue the ability of intermediate dimer mutants to bind γTuRC, suggesting that simply bringing mutants into proximity is insufficient to restore proper γTuRC binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing SEC traces confirming dimerization rescue but Western blots showing no rescue of γTuRC binding. This negative result provides important mechanistic insight into the requirements for γTuRC binding.

results.result: In extract, wildtype γTuNA activates MT nucleation while F75A and L77A mutants have no effect. The I67A mutant activates to ~50% of wildtype levels, but L70A has no activity despite retaining ~35% binding ability, suggesting a threshold for γTuRC activation in extract.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing TIRF microscopy quantification of MT nucleation in extract (N=4 biological replicates). The divergence between L70A's binding ability and activation effect provides important insight into the requirements for functional activation.

results.result: In vitro, γTuNA triggers a 5-fold increase in MT mass and a ~20-fold increase in γTuRC nucleation rate (from 1.2 to 24.5 MTs/s), with minimal effect on MT growth speed or length. The effect is almost exclusively due to direct increase in γTuRC activity, not altered MT dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by comprehensive quantitative analysis in Figure 5 including MT mass, nucleation rate, growth speed, and length measurements from multiple biological replicates (N=6-8). The data clearly demonstrate that γTuNA's primary effect is on nucleation rate rather than MT dynamics.

results.result: Bulky N-terminal tags on γTuNA completely ablate its ability to activate γTuRC, instead turning it into a specific γTuRC repressor.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing inhibition of MT nucleation with N-terminally Halo-tagged γTuNA in both extract and in vitro. This finding has important implications for experimental design and interpretation of prior studies.

results.result: F75A and L77A mutants have no significant effect on initial γTuRC nucleation rate in vitro. However, L77A shows a weakly significant late increase in MT number (beginning at 150s) and a 1.4-fold increase in nucleation rate, behavior not observed in extract, suggesting that extract factors block impaired dimer mutants from stimulating γTuRC.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing quantitative analysis of MT nucleation over time. The divergent behavior of L77A in extract versus in vitro provides important mechanistic insight, though the statistical significance of the L77A effect is weak (p~0.03).

results.result: A simple deterministic model based on initial nucleation rates captures most of the behavior in the system except for L77A. The model demonstrates that wildtype γTuNA's effect is due to direct increase in γTuRC activity without altering MT dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by simulation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 showing good agreement between simulated and experimental data for wildtype and F75A. The model provides additional support for the conclusion that γTuNA primarily affects nucleation rate. However, the two-phase model for L77A (C68) is more speculative.

results.result: At double and triple endogenous stathmin concentrations (~3-4.2 μM), there is drastic loss of MT nucleation in extract. However, γTuNA still activates MT nucleation even at the highest stathmin concentration tested, with a ~5-fold increase in MT number.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6A-B showing TIRF microscopy quantification of MT nucleation in extract with varying stathmin concentrations (N=4 biological replicates). The data demonstrate that γTuNA activation can overcome stathmin inhibition.

results.result: In vitro, stathmin causes 59% and 81% loss of MT mass at 2.5 or 4 μM respectively. Addition of γTuNA rescues MT mass, restoring levels to the γTuRC control at 4 μM stathmin. This suggests γTuNA indirectly counteracts stathmin by increasing efficiency of γTuRC-mediated MT nucleation at lower tubulin concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6C-D showing quantitative analysis of MT mass in vitro with stathmin and γTuNA (N=3-5 biological replicates). The rescue of MT mass by γTuNA provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: At γTuRC's critical tubulin concentration (7 μM), γTuRC has minimal activity (~1-2 MTs over 5 minutes). In the presence of γTuNA, γTuRC activity increases 25-fold, demonstrating that γTuNA decreases γTuRC's critical tubulin concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6E showing TIRF microscopy quantification at low tubulin concentration. The 25-fold increase in activity provides strong evidence that γTuNA enhances γTuRC's ability to nucleate MTs at lower tubulin concentrations.

results.result: The study demonstrates that γTuNA is an obligate dimer requiring both dimerization and F75 for γTuRC binding, providing first biochemical validation of recent structural data. γTuNA dimers directly activate γTuRC-dependent MT nucleation in extract and in vitro, and overcome barriers posed by stathmin. Findings are broadly applicable as γTuNA domains are found in multiple proteins across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented in Figures 1-6. The combination of extract experiments, in vitro reconstitution, mutagenesis, and quantitative analysis provides strong support for these conclusions. The claim of 'first biochemical validation' (C82) is supported by the experimental data and citation to prior structural work.

results.result: The manuscript discusses possible mechanisms for γTuNA activation, noting that prior structural studies observed no obvious conformational change, suggesting γTuNA may only transiently bias γTuRC toward closed conformation. Prior modeling suggested tubulin binding provides sufficient energy to overcome the open-to-closed barrier, and γTuNA may lower this barrier as evidenced by decreased critical tubulin concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are largely speculative (C87, C89, C90) and based on inference from current experimental data combined with prior structural and modeling studies. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by the observation that γTuNA lowers critical tubulin concentration, direct structural evidence for the proposed mechanism is lacking.

results.result: Recent work in yeast suggests that near-closure of γTuRC might require simultaneous binding by multiple CM1/γTuNA domains. Yeast γTuRC has six well-defined CM1/γTuNA binding sites, suggesting additional sites may exist in vertebrate γTuRCs, though none have been detected yet.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by citation to prior published work (Brilot et al., 2021). Claims C93-C94 appropriately distinguish between what is known (yeast structure) and what is speculative (additional sites in vertebrates). The speculation is reasonable but clearly identified as such.

results.result: The proposed model involves direct binding between dimerized γTuNA-containing proteins and γTuRC, activating nucleation ~20-fold and overcoming negative regulation by stathmin or low tubulin. Activated γTuRCs are enriched at MTOCs via additional localization motifs, with regulation via phosphorylation preventing ectopic activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by the experimental data presented in the study. Claim C98 is more speculative but supported by citations to prior work on phosphorylation regulation. The model integrates the current findings with established knowledge about Cdk5rap2 localization and regulation.

results.result: An estimated 33% of purified γTuRCs retain a γTuNA dimer after purification, meaning the baseline γTuRC activity is likely higher than with γTuNA-independent purification. This suggests γTuNA dimers might have an even more potent effect than reported.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C showing Western blot-based quantification. Claims C100-C101 are reasonable inferences from this observation, though C101 is somewhat speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and its implications for interpreting their results.

results.result: The region from position 75-77 (F75, L77) is the core γTuNA-γTuRC binding interface. Mutations moving from this core toward the N-terminus (L70 to I67 to F63) have progressively less impact on dimerization and γTuRC binding. The divergent behavior of L70A and L77A reflects L70's position outside the most critical region, though L70A's residual binding is insufficient for significant activation in extract.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing systematic analysis of mutants at different positions. The interpretation is based on inference from the data but is well-supported by the observed correlation between position and functional effect.

results.result: The I67A/L70A double mutant retains some γTuRC binding despite strong loss of dimerization, but double substitution to aspartate (I67D/L70D) completely removes binding. This suggests retaining some hydrophobicity preserves enough coil structure for weak γTuRC interaction. SEC data showing different retention volumes for I67D/L70D versus I67A/L70A supports structural changes with hydrophilic substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C111 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing Western blots and SEC traces. The interpretation involves inference about structural changes, but is well-supported by the quantitative differences in retention volumes and binding abilities between alanine and aspartate substitutions.

results.result: The manuscript proposes that two separate monomeric coils of mutant γTuNA might bind the same γTuRC and form a weak complex, with γTuRC interaction stabilizing the dimer. This explains the late effect of L77A in vitro but not in extract, suggesting extract factors compete against this interaction. Weak binding may only occur with hydrophobic-to-weaker-hydrophobic substitutions that don't drastically alter coil structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 are largely speculative, though based on reasonable inference from experimental data showing divergent behavior of mutants in extract versus in vitro. The proposed mechanism for L77A's late activation is plausible but lacks direct experimental validation. The speculation is clearly identified and appropriately tentative.

results.result: The γTuNA-GCN4 fusion constructs did not rescue γTuRC binding despite rescuing dimerization, likely because the GCN4 domain did not restore local coil structure or hydrophobic character of the core region. This suggests specific residues are required for both dimerization and making specific contacts with γTuRC, and that core residues like L77 have dual impacts on both processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1. Claims C122-C124 involve inference and speculation but are reasonable interpretations of the negative result. The discussion appropriately distinguishes between what is demonstrated and what is inferred.

results.result: Dimerization is a key component of γTuNA-γTuRC interaction but is not sufficient on its own. The F75 residue, located on the outer surface of the dimer, is required for activation and strong binding in all assays, likely having a stabilizing or docking role to 'lock' γTuNA into γTuRC.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 are supported by experimental data throughout Figures 1-5 and citation to prior structural work. Claim C128 is speculative but represents a reasonable interpretation of F75's role based on its position and functional importance. The distinction between demonstrated facts and speculation is clear.

results.result: The manuscript addresses apparent discrepancies with prior work by Liu et al., noting they used N-terminally GST-tagged γTuNA and observed minimal activation effect. The current study finds that large N-terminal tags do not interfere with γTuRC binding but bulky Halo-tags turn γTuNA into a specific inhibitor, likely due to steric clash. Differences in tag distance and γTuNA:γTuRC ratio may determine whether activation is possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C137 are supported by citations to prior work and experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The explanation for divergent results is reasonable and supported by the inhibition data. The discussion appropriately considers multiple factors that could explain differences between studies.

results.result: The manuscript explains that N-terminally 6xHis-tagged γTuNA activates MT nucleation in extract but had little effect on the original antibody-purified γTuRC in vitro. The new Halo-γTuNA purification method provides at least 20-fold higher yield and purity with more robust activity, resulting in better detection of γTuNA's activation effect. The difference is attributed to improved γTuRC quality rather than additional factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C144 are supported by experimental data comparing the new and old purification methods, including silver stain analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B. The explanation for improved detection of γTuNA's effect is reasonable and supported by the data, validating and extending prior work by the Qi group.

results.result: Mass spectrometry detected NME7 as a γTuRC subunit, consistent with prior work. Three unique proteins (CDK1 subunits A and B, and CAMK2D) were enriched at higher levels than NME7 and had not been reported to interact with γTuRC or γTuNA, suggesting they might be novel co-factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C148 are supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. However, claim C149 is speculative - while the proteins are enriched, additional validation would be needed to confirm they are bona fide γTuRC co-factors rather than non-specific binders or contaminants. The speculation is appropriately tentative.
